title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Which treatment process changes a pollutant’s chemical form, and which transfers it into a stream that still needs to be managed?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Learning goals

Match a chemical form to an appropriate treatment mechanism.
Calculate sequential load transfers and distinguish transformation from removal.
Use reaction stoichiometry to explain oxygen and alkalinity requirements.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Start with the target form
Particles, dissolved ions, neutral organic molecules, and microorganisms behave differently. Settling or filtration can remove particles while leaving many dissolved species. Coagulation changes particle interactions and can capture some colloidal or associated dissolved material. Sorption transfers selected molecules to a solid. A treatment choice must specify the target, its form, and a receiving phase; one generic removal percentage cannot apply to all pollutants.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Precipitation and sorption transfer material
Metal or phosphate precipitation depends on pH, free-ion activities, solid identity, and competing ligands. Coagulant hydrolysis can generate acidity; simplified \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+3H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s)+3H^+}\) shows why alkalinity matters. The actual precipitate and net reaction depend on conditions. Settled sludge retains the transferred element and requires management. A fall in water concentration is not elemental destruction.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Biological oxidation changes species
Aerobic organic oxidation consumes oxygen and produces inorganic carbon. Nitrification oxidises ammonium to nitrate, consumes oxygen, and generates acidity. Nitrate is still dissolved nitrogen. Denitrification can convert nitrate to N₂ when a suitable electron donor and conditions are present. These are chemical balances behind treatment functions, not a full reactor design or a promise of complete conversion in every plant.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Sequential percentages multiply
A second treatment stage acts on the mass entering that stage, not the original mass unless specified. If stage one removes fraction \(f_1\) and stage two removes \(f_2\) of the remainder, water retains \(M_0(1-f_1)(1-f_2)\). Keep separate balances for effluent, solids, gas, and transformed products. Adding percentage removals can exceed 100% and obscures where the material goes.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Disinfection and residuals
Disinfection addresses viable microorganisms; it does not automatically remove chemical contaminants. Oxidants can react with organic matter and create transformation products, so target inactivation and chemical byproducts need separate evaluation. This course explains the mechanisms and balances; treatment protocols, dosing, and performance criteria require the actual system and its operating evidence.

title: Water pollution and treatment chemistry
text:
Worked example
Start with 10.0 mg of an element in a tracked water volume. Stage one transfers 60.0% to solids: 6.00 mg solid and 4.00 mg water. Stage two transfers 50.0% of the remaining water inventory: 2.00 mg more solid and 2.00 mg effluent. Total transfer is 80.0%, and 8.00 + 2.00 = 10.0 mg closes the element balance. This example assumes no gas or chemical-product stream.

Two stages each remove 30.0% of the entering water-phase mass. Start with 100 mg. Find final water mass and overall removal.

2. Coagulant acidity
Assume 0.0200 mmol/L Fe³⁺ undergoes the supplied hydroxide precipitation reaction completely. Calculate H⁺ generation and the equivalent alkalinity decrease.






Hint





Each mole Fe³⁺ produces three moles H⁺ in this representation.

3. Track nitrogen
A process changes 1.00 mmol/L NH₄⁺ into 1.00 mmol/L NO₃⁻, with no other nitrogen products. Has it removed nitrogen? What process could remove dissolved nitrogen as gas?






Hint





Compare nitrogen atoms across forms.

4. Choose and justify
A water contains suspended clay, dissolved nitrate, and a neutral organic contaminant. Explain why filtration alone is not a complete treatment argument.






Hint





Match particle size and chemical form to mechanism.









Worked solution

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
If a contaminant disappears from water, is it removed from the environmental system or transferred onto a mobile particle?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Learning goals

Explain pH-dependent surface charge and specific binding.
Close a water–solid mass balance using a supplied Kd.
Distinguish sorption equilibrium, finite capacity, and colloidal transport.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
A surface is chemically active
Oxide surfaces carry hydroxyl groups that can gain or lose protons. Schematically, \(\mathrm{>SOH+H^+\rightleftharpoons >SOH_2^+}\) and \(\mathrm{>SOH\rightleftharpoons >SO^-+H^+}\). Here >S denotes a surface site, not dissolved sulfur. Some clay charge arises from crystal substitutions and is less directly pH dependent. Surface charge influences electrostatic attraction, while specific ligand exchange can bind solutes beyond a simple opposite-charge picture.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Define a distribution coefficient
In a linear equilibrium approximation, \(q=K_dC_w\), where \(q\) is sorbed mass per dry solid mass (mg/kg), \(C_w\) is aqueous concentration (mg/L), and \(K_d\) is L/kg. State the measurement conditions. The coefficient can change with pH, competing solutes, and concentration. It is not a universal molecular constant and should not be applied outside its range without evidence.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Close the two-phase balance
For a closed bottle with water volume \(V_w\) L, dry solid mass \(m_s\) kg, and total solute mass \(M_T\) mg, \[M_T=C_wV_w+qm_s=C_w(V_w+K_dm_s).\] Thus \(C_w=M_T/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). The sorbed fraction is \(K_dm_s/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). The denominator has litre units in both terms. The model excludes degradation, wall loss, and non-equilibrium transport.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Capacity and competition
A linear model has no finite saturation plateau. A Langmuir teaching model, \(q=q_{max}bC/(1+bC)\), approaches a limiting capacity \(q_{max}\). Real surfaces can have several kinds of sites and hysteresis. Phosphate can bind to iron oxides, but competition, site occupation, mineral changes, and pH alter retention. A low-concentration Kd should not be extrapolated to unlimited loading.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Particles may move
Sorption onto settling solids can retain a solute locally, but sorption onto mobile colloids can assist transport. Operational filtration does not perfectly separate a dissolved molecular pool from every particle size. Particle settling, aggregation, and resuspension change the boundary fluxes. To claim removal, identify the destination and whether it remains outside the receiving water over the relevant timescale.



Predicted equilibrium water concentration as dry solid mass increases in a closed bottle.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption
text:
Worked example
Distribute 1.00 mg between 1.00 L water and 0.0100 kg dry solid, with \(K_d=100\) L/kg. Then \(K_dm_s=1.00\) L, \(C_w=1.00/(1.00+1.00)=\mathbf{0.500}\) mg/L, and \(q=50.0\) mg/kg. Water contains 0.500 mg and solid contains 0.500 mg. The total stays 1.00 mg. Half is sorbed; none has been destroyed.

1. Double the solid
Repeat the worked example with 0.0200 kg solid, keeping all other inputs fixed. Find aqueous concentration and both inventories.






Hint





Use the full denominator, not a proportional guess.

Cw = 1/(1 + 100 × 0.0200) = 0.3333 mg/L. Water holds 0.3333 mg, solid 0.6667 mg. The sorbed concentration is 33.33 mg/kg and the total remains 1.00 mg.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
2. A loading limit
A solid has qmax = 20.0 mg/kg and dry mass 0.0100 kg. Can it bind 1.00 mg on those sites?






Hint





Multiply capacity by dry solid mass.









Worked solution





The maximum site inventory is 0.200 mg, so 1.00 mg cannot all bind there. More solid, other retention mechanisms, or a larger aqueous pool would be required.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
3. A desorption change
A new pH changes Kd in the original bottle from 100 to 10.0 L/kg. At equilibrium with the same total mass and volume, what is Cw?






Hint





Changing Kd redistributes the fixed inventory.









Worked solution





Cw = 1/(1 + 10 × 0.0100) = 0.9091 mg/L. Aqueous mass is 0.9091 mg and sorbed mass 0.09091 mg. Desorption raised the water concentration without adding total solute.

title: Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises
text:
4. Removal or transport?
A filtered sample loses metal while the unfiltered downstream sample does not. How could particles explain this observation?






Hint





Compare operational fractions and whether particles settle or remain mobile.









Worked solution





Metal may bind to particles excluded by filtration while remaining in the moving water-plus-particle system. Measure particle loads, size fractions, flow, and phase inventories. A filtered concentration decrease alone does not establish destruction or permanent retention.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
When oxygen runs low, why can iron, nitrogen, sulfur, and phosphorus change together even though not every element changes oxidation state?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Learning goals

Balance a redox reaction using electron transfer.
Interpret electron-acceptor evidence without assuming a universal sequence.
Connect iron-phase changes to associated phosphate release.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Electron donors and acceptors
Organic matter can supply electrons as its carbon is oxidised. Electron acceptors such as O₂, nitrate, iron(III) solids, and sulfate are reduced. The oxidation and reduction half-reactions must transfer equal numbers of electrons. \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) is a useful carbon-oxidation bookkeeping form, not a claim that every substrate has that composition. Electron balance constrains possible stoichiometry; microbes and transport control the realised rate.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
A nitrogen contrast
Aerobic nitrification has net stoichiometry \[\mathrm{NH_4^++2O_2\rightarrow NO_3^-+2H^++H_2O}.\] Nitrogen is oxidised from −III to +V. In contrast, denitrification reduces nitrate to N₂; with a CH₂O donor one net form is \[\mathrm{4NO_3^-+5CH_2O+4H^+\rightarrow2N_2+5CO_2+7H_2O}.\] These net reactions omit biomass growth and intermediate pathways. Nitrification changes nitrogen form; denitrification can export nitrogen from water as gas.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
section: Iron reduction changes a solid phase
text:
Iron reduction changes a solid phase
For goethite-like FeOOH, use the reduction half-reaction \[\mathrm{FeOOH(s)+3H^++e^-\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2H_2O}.\] The iron(III) solid becomes dissolved iron(II) under this simplified representation. If phosphate was retained on that solid, dissolving or restructuring it can release phosphate without changing phosphorus from oxidation state +V. Other solids, sorption sites, or precipitation reactions may retain some released solute.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Sulfur and strongly reducing conditions
Sulfate reduction can be written as \[\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}+9H^++8e^-\rightarrow HS^-+4H_2O}.\] Sulfide can react with metals to form low-solubility solids, changing mobility again. Reduced sulfur can later reoxidise if oxygen returns. Thus anoxia does not mean every metal becomes permanently dissolved, and reoxygenation does not simply reverse every process at the same speed.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Interpret a redox sequence
A common conceptual progression is oxygen use, nitrate reduction, manganese/iron reduction, sulfate reduction, and methanogenesis. It is a guide to possible energy and availability constraints, not a universal timetable or a single set of pH-independent thresholds. Spatial microsites and transport allow processes to overlap. An electrode potential alone seldom identifies all active processes in a mixed natural sample; combine reactant loss with product formation and solid-phase evidence.

title: Redox and environmental cycles
text:
Worked example
In the supplied CH₂O–nitrate reaction, each nitrate N goes from +V to 0 and gains five electrons. Four nitrate ions therefore accept 20 electrons. Carbon goes from 0 in CH₂O to +IV in CO₂ and loses four electrons; five CH₂O units donate 20. Both sides contain 4 N, 5 C, 14 H, and 17 O atoms and have net charge zero. The donor ratio is 1.25 mol CH₂O carbon per mol nitrate in this model.

1. Nitrification acid demand
Oxidise 0.100 mmol/L NH₄⁺ completely to nitrate using the supplied reaction. Find O₂ demand and H⁺ production.

Use the balanced coefficients 1:2:2.

2. Denitrification donor
Reduce 0.0800 mmol/L nitrate entirely to N₂ with the CH₂O model. Find organic carbon consumption and N₂ production.






Hint





Use five CH₂O and two N₂ for four nitrate.

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises

3. Check a half-reaction
Verify atoms and charge for FeOOH + 3 H⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ + 2 H₂O. What is reduced?






Hint





FeOOH contains one hydrogen and two oxygens.

Both sides have 1 Fe, 2 O, and 4 H. Left charge is +3 − 1 = +2, matching right charge. Fe(III) gains one electron to become Fe(II).

title: Redox and environmental cycles exercises
text:
4. An anoxic sediment observation
Dissolved iron and phosphate rise while oxygen declines above a sediment. Give a coupled explanation and one reason it is not proven by correlation alone.






Hint





The carrier phase can change oxidation state while phosphate retains its own oxidation state.









Worked solution





Organic-matter oxidation can consume O₂ and support reduction of Fe(III) solids; associated phosphate can be released. Mixing, other mineral changes, and independent sources could also produce patterns. Use Fe(II), solid-phase, porewater, and time/flux observations to test the explanation.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Which linked chemical explanation survives the available balances, and which parts remain hypotheses?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Learning goals

Combine deposition, neutralisation, and water export in one equivalent budget.
Use several indicators to assess a coupled sediment-redox explanation.
Write a reproducible chemical explanation that separates model predictions from observations.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
The annual catchment budget
Reuse the constructed catchment: area \(1.00\times10^6\) m², annual water export \(5.00\times10^8\) L, and acid-equivalent input 40000 eq/year. A stipulated mineral/soil neutralisation term consumes 30000 eq/year. With no other acid terms in this teaching budget, residual export is 10000 eq/year or 0.0200 meq/L. Do not silently add unmeasured retention or biological terms to force agreement.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: An alkalinity comparison needs a reference
text:
An alkalinity comparison needs a reference
For an explicit comparison, suppose reference annual alkalinity export is 50000 eq/year under the same water export, and the added residual acidity decreases it by 10000 eq/year. Alkalinity then changes from 0.100 to 0.0800 meq/L. This does not fix pH: dissolved inorganic carbon, gas exchange, and other acid–base systems are still needed. An annual flow-weighted export is not the same boundary condition as the closed-water acid pulse in the carbonate unit.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
A separate sediment observation set
A second constructed comparison samples water immediately above sediment before and during oxygen depletion. O₂ changes from 8.0 to 0.20 mg/L; filtered Fe from 0.020 to 1.00 mg/L; filtered phosphate-P from 0.010 to 0.200 mg P/L. These are invented observations, not outputs of a fitted reaction model. They are consistent with reduction of an iron carrier phase and associated phosphate release, but do not identify that mechanism uniquely.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Keep forms and units aligned
Phosphate-P is reported as elemental phosphorus mass, not phosphate-ion mass. Filtered Fe is not automatically free Fe²⁺. Annual acidity is an equivalent flux; pH is a present activity measure. Before combining evidence, state whether measurements refer to matching water masses, times, and operational fractions. A neat numerical correlation can be chemically meaningless if quantities or boundaries differ.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
section: Build an explanation with a test
text:
Build an explanation with a test
An explanation should give the proposed reaction chain, a supporting balance or calculation, a prediction, and a measurement that could distinguish alternatives. For the catchment, compare neutralisation, alkalinity export, major ions, and flow. For sediment, test Fe(II), mineral phases, porewater gradients, and solute fluxes. Alternative sources and mixing belong in the interpretation when the available observations cannot rule them out.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water
text:
Worked example
If neutralisation were only 20000 instead of 30000 eq/year, the residual input would be 20000 eq/year = 0.0400 meq/L at the stated export. Under the same 50000 eq/year reference alkalinity, export would be 30000 eq/year = 0.0600 meq/L. This is a sensitivity calculation: it shows which term controls the budget. It does not establish which catchment process changed or predict a unique pH.

text:
1. Close the annual budget
Calculate residual acidity and reference-adjusted alkalinity export for the base case. Report annual equivalents and meq/L.






Hint





Work in annual equivalents before converting to a flow-weighted concentration.









Worked solution





Residual acidity = 10000 eq/year, or 0.0200 meq/L. Alkalinity export = 50000 − 10000 = 40000 eq/year, or 0.0800 meq/L. No pH follows without additional constraints.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises

Double water export to 1.00 × 10⁹ L/year, holding acid and neutralisation amounts fixed only for this sensitivity exercise. Find residual acid-equivalent concentration. Is it reasonable to assume all real catchment processes stay unchanged?






Hint





Divide the same annual residual by the new annual volume.









Worked solution





Residual concentration is 0.0100 meq/L. In a real catchment, higher water flow could change weathering contact, retention, and transport. The fixed-flux sensitivity is an explicit mathematical assumption, not a universal hydrological response.

title: Connecting air, catchments, and water exercises

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
How does an atmospheric emission become an acid input to a catchment, and why does rain pH alone not give the annual acid load?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Learning goals

Trace oxidation and wet/dry transfer from air to a catchment.
Convert a deposition flux to amount and charge equivalents.
Distinguish free hydrogen ion, potential acidity, and net catchment response.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Oxidation creates new species
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are precursors, not simply bottles of sulfuric and nitric acid dispersed in air. Oxidation occurs through several gas and aqueous pathways. One useful nitrogen pathway is \(\mathrm{NO_2+OH+M\rightarrow HNO_3+M}\). A net sulfur oxidation can be represented as \(\mathrm{SO_2+\tfrac12O_2+H_2O\rightarrow H_2SO_4}\); this is bookkeeping, not an elementary rate law.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Wet and dry pathways
Wet deposition transfers substances in rain, snow, fog, or cloud water. Dry deposition transfers gases and particles to surfaces without precipitation. Aerosols are suspended particles or droplets; some are emitted and others form by chemical reactions. A low rain concentration during a wet year can still correspond to a large wet flux. Dry deposition requires separate information and cannot be inferred just from a rain sample.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Count acid equivalents carefully
In a stated complete neutralisation convention, HNO₃ supplies one equivalent per mole and H₂SO₄ supplies two. Actual deposited sulfate or nitrate need not arrive as free acid: accompanying cations, ammonium, and biological transformations matter. Ammonia can neutralise atmospheric acid; later nitrification of ammonium can generate acidity. Do not assign two free hydrogen ions to every measured sulfate regardless of its chemical form.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
section: Connect flux to a receiving volume
text:
Connect flux to a receiving volume
For a uniform flux \(F\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ and catchment area \(A\), the annual input is \(FA\). Converting that input to an equivalent water concentration requires a receiving water volume and assumptions about retention, export, and mixing. In the recurring teaching catchment, use area \(1.00\times10^6\) m² and annual water export \(5.00\times10^8\) L. This defines an annual flow-weighted concentration, not a sudden dose to a closed lake.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Why catchments respond differently
Weathering, mineral availability, soil exchange, plant uptake, and flow paths modify the relationship between atmospheric input and lake chemistry. pH describes the current hydrogen-ion activity; alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance. A buffered catchment can receive acid while showing a modest pH change. Measurements should therefore link atmospheric fluxes with water flow, alkalinity, and major ions rather than treating pH as a complete budget.

title: Atmospheric deposition and acidity
text:
Worked example
Assume the catchment receives \(0.0200\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ of HNO₃ and \(0.0100\) mol m⁻² yr⁻¹ of H₂SO₄, with full neutralisation of both protons in the stated accounting convention. The acid-equivalent flux is \(0.0200+2(0.0100)=0.0400\) eq m⁻² yr⁻¹. Over \(1.00\times10^6\) m², that is 40000 eq/year. If an identified catchment neutralisation process consumes 30000 eq/year and no other acid terms act, the residual is 10000 eq/year. Dividing by \(5.00\times10^8\) L/year gives 0.0200 meq/L of residual equivalent load. This budget is constructed; it does not predict pH without carbonate and other constraints.

Inputs are 0.100 and 1.00 mmol H⁺/m². The larger event carries ten times the free hydrogen-ion amount. Other acid–base species and dry deposition are not included.

Counterions and subsequent transformations affect acidity.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Species and equilibria
Write \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\) for \(\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\). It is a combined pool, not the chemical formula of a single molecule. Most of this pool is dissolved molecular carbon dioxide under these conditions. The effective first dissociation incorporates hydration:
\[\mathrm{CO_2^* + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-},\qquad
K_1=10^{-6.35}.\]
\[\mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + CO_3^{2-}},\qquad
K_2=10^{-10.33}.\]
In the first expression, the water term represents the net reaction of dissolved carbon dioxide; the notation groups hydrated and unhydrated forms together.
The total dissolved inorganic carbon in this model is
\[C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}].\]
No carbon leaves this sum merely because it changes species. Mineral reactions, gas exchange, or biological transformations can change the dissolved total.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
section: Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
text:
Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
Dividing the equilibrium expressions gives
\[r_1=\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35},\qquad
r_2=\frac{[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-10.33}.\]
The proportions of the three species are \(1:r_1:r_1r_2\). Therefore
\[\alpha_0=\frac{1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_1=\frac{r_1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_2=\frac{r_1r_2}{1+r_1+r_1r_2}.\]
Each \(\alpha\) is dimensionless and each concentration is \(\alpha_i C_T\). The fractions sum to one. In this model the fractions depend on pH and the constants; \(C_T\) sets the concentration scale. A distribution curve supplies possible compositions at prescribed pH values. It does not solve for pH.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Alkalinity and buffering
The carbonate-only total alkalinity is
\[A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}],\qquad
[\mathrm{OH^-}]=K_w/[\mathrm{H^+}].\]
Use mol of charge equivalents per litre (eq/L); \(1\) meq/L is \(10^{-3}\) eq/L. Bicarbonate contributes one equivalent per mole, carbonate two. Real freshwater can have additional alkalinity contributions, so this expression must be checked before applying it to measurements. The USGS carbonate-speciation guidance explains the importance of other acid-neutralising species.
Alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance relative to the carbon dioxide reference state. pH describes hydrogen-ion activity at the present state. Local buffer capacity describes the amount of acid or base required for a small pH change under specified conditions. These are related, but are different quantities.
For a strong-acid addition \(q\) eq/L with negligible dilution and no other reaction, \(A_{T,\mathrm{after}}=A_{T,\mathrm{before}}-q\). In a closed water with no mineral or biological reactions, \(C_T\) stays constant. Added acid redistributes carbon toward \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\). The final pH must satisfy both the carbon balance and the new alkalinity.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Gas and mineral boundaries
For water equilibrated with a large gas reservoir, use the specified convention
\[[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=K_H p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}.\]
Here partial pressure is in atm. Applying this coefficient to total inorganic carbon would be incorrect. Gas uptake by itself changes \(C_T\) but conserves \(A_T\) in our model. At fixed alkalinity it generally lowers pH. Fixing gas pressure, pH, and \(C_T\) independently would usually overconstrain the model.
For calcite, \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+CO_3^{2-}}\). Use the free-ion concentrations to estimate
\[\Omega=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{K_{sp}}.\]
\(\Omega<1\) indicates undersaturation; dissolution is thermodynamically favoured if calcite is available. \(\Omega>1\) indicates supersaturation; precipitation can be favoured, but kinetics and nucleation can delay it. \(\Omega=1\) is saturation. Dissolving one mole of calcite adds one mole to dissolved inorganic carbon and two equivalents to alkalinity. This process is excluded from the closed acid example.

One element, three dissolved pools

Changing species redistributes carbon. It does not itself remove dissolved carbon.

\mathrm{CO_2^*+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H^++HCO_3^-} \mathrm{HCO_3^-\rightleftharpoons H^++CO_3^{2-}}

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
2. Same pH, different acid response
Two constructed waters start at pH 7.50. Water A has \(C_T=1.00\) mmol/L; water B has \(C_T=0.100\) mmol/L. At this pH the fractions are \(\alpha_0=0.066023\), \(\alpha_1=0.932598\), \(\alpha_2=0.001379\).

Calculate initial alkalinity from the carbonate-only expression. Include water ions: \([\mathrm{H^+}]=3.1623\times10^{-8}\) mol/L and \([\mathrm{OH^-}]=3.1623\times10^{-7}\) mol/L.
Add 0.0500 mmol/L of a strong monoprotic acid to each, with negligible dilution. Calculate each new alkalinity. No gas exchange, mineral reaction, or biological transformation occurs. What happens to \(C_T\)?
A calculation satisfying both balances gives final pH values 7.235 for A and 6.252 for B. Explain the difference without assuming initial pH measures the acid-neutralising inventory.
Can you obtain the final pH by subtracting 0.0500 from 7.50? Explain the units.







Hint





First put all concentrations in mol/L. Multiply the carbonate concentration by two in the alkalinity expression. A mole of monoprotic strong acid supplies one equivalent. To express eq/L as meq/L, multiply by 1000.









Worked solution





For A, the bicarbonate and carbonate contribution is \((0.932598+2\times0.001379)\times10^{-3}\) eq/L. The water-ion term is \(2.8461\times10^{-7}\) eq/L. The resulting initial alkalinities are approximately 0.9356 meq/L for A and 0.09382 meq/L for B.
The acid supplies 0.0500 meq/L. Final alkalinities are therefore 0.8856 and 0.04382 meq/L. Carbon stays dissolved in this closed model, so each \(C_T\) is conserved; a larger fraction becomes CO₂*.
B loses about 53% of its initial alkalinity, compared with about 5.3% for A. Its larger pH fall is consistent with its smaller carbonate inventory. Alkalinity is not identical to local buffer capacity, but here the two waters have the same initial species fractions and different carbon amounts.
A pH difference is logarithmic and dimensionless; an acid dose has amount-per-volume units. Direct subtraction cannot satisfy the chemical balances. A numerical solver is not required for this exercise.

Is that enough information to calculate pH or \(C_T\)?
If the equilibrated water is also specified to have pH 8.35, calculate \(C_T\).
In another water, CO₂ enters while no acid, mineral, or biological process acts. Explain why the alkalinity stays constant even though pH can decrease.







Worked solution





\([\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=0.034\times4.00\times10^{-4}=1.36\times10^{-5}\) mol/L = 13.6 µmol/L. The atm units cancel. This specifies the gas pool only. Another independent carbonate constraint is needed to calculate pH and total carbon.
With pH 8.35 supplied, \(C_T=13.6(1+100+1.04713)\) µmol/L, or approximately 1.388 mmol/L. Henry’s law alone did not give that total.
Dissociation of the added CO₂ produces hydrogen ion and bicarbonate together; their contributions cancel in alkalinity. Gas transfer adds carbon rather than strong-acid equivalents. At fixed alkalinity the pH generally falls as CO₂ enters. An imposed pH of 8.35 is a specified state, not the predicted endpoint of every water exposed to this gas.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
4. Check calcite saturation
Two separate water states each have free calcium \(5.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. Free carbonate is \(1.00\times10^{-6}\) mol/L in state X and \(1.00\times10^{-5}\) mol/L in state Y. Use \(K_{sp}=3.3\times10^{-9}\).
Calculate \(\Omega\) for each. Identify which could dissolve available calcite and which could precipitate it. Can you infer a precipitation rate or final mass? Explain why replacing free calcium with dissolved total calcium might matter.






Worked solution





The products are \(5.00\times10^{-10}\) and \(5.00\times10^{-9}\). Thus \(\Omega_X=0.152\) and \(\Omega_Y=1.52\). X is undersaturated and could dissolve calcite if it is present. Y is supersaturated, so precipitation is thermodynamically favoured, but may be delayed by kinetics or nucleation. Neither ratio gives a rate or final mass. Ion pairs and complexes can make free calcium smaller than total dissolved calcium.

section: 5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
text:
5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
This task reuses objects, arithmetic, tables, and labelled plots from introductory computing. The small addition is a regular pH grid. No statistical fit is needed: these are predictions from equilibrium expressions.
Download speciation.R and report.Rmd into the same folder. Open that folder as your working project. The script needs ggplot2; rendering the report also needs rmarkdown, as in introductory computing. Open the script in the editor before running it.

Predict and inspect
Before running the script, sketch the expected dominance near pH 4, 8, and 12. The script starts with these calculations:
pH <- seq(4, 12, by = 0.05)
r1 <- 10^(pH - 6.35)
r2 <- 10^(pH - 10.33)
denominator <- 1 + r1 + r1 * r2
seq() creates regularly spaced values. Each vector operation evaluates the chemical expression at every pH value. ^ means a power. The script divides the three proportions by denominator and puts them in a table. Its remaining code arranges that table for the familiar ggplot() and geom_line() functions.
Run from the folder holding both files:
source("speciation.R")
head(speciation)
speciation_plot
Compare the plot with the prediction and with the hand calculation in question 1.



Three carbonate species fractions at prescribed pH, calculated from the supplied equilibrium model.




Check and explain

In the report template, select the pH 8.35 row and compare its fractions with your hand calculation. Explain any difference due to rounding.
Check that fractions stay between zero and one and sum to one.
Explain what happens to concentrations if \(C_T\) doubles at each prescribed pH.
Explain why moving along the horizontal axis does not simulate adding a specified dose of acid to a closed sample.
Replace the template prompts with your prediction, calculation, chemical interpretation, and assumptions. Restart R, then Knit the saved report, or run rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd") from its folder.







Worked interpretation





CO₂* dominates at low pH, bicarbonate in the middle, and carbonate at high pH. At pH 8.35, the model fractions agree with question 1. The sum is one to numerical precision, and every fraction lies between zero and one. Doubling \(C_T\) at fixed pH doubles the concentrations, while leaving these model fractions unchanged.
The horizontal axis supplies pH independently at each point. An acid-dose experiment must instead conserve carbon and satisfy the changed alkalinity. The curve alone does not supply that second constraint or predict a final pH. The model assumes equilibrium, 25 °C, and dilute freshwater; it omits ion pairing and other acid–base systems.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
6. Explain a catchment observation
A lake’s pH decreases after a disturbance. Suggest two chemically distinct processes from this unit that could cause a decrease, and identify additional measurements that would help distinguish them. State one limitation of interpreting only pH. Do not claim a cause from a single observation.






Worked explanation





Strong-acid input and net CO₂ uptake can both lower pH. In the isolated model, strong acid lowers alkalinity while CO₂ uptake conserves it and increases dissolved inorganic carbon. Paired pH, alkalinity, and inorganic-carbon or dissolved-CO₂ measurements would help assess these possibilities. Calcium and mineral context could reveal additional reactions. A real catchment can have several processes acting together; pH alone does not identify the cause or neutralising inventory.

Learning goals

Distinguish organic carbon amount from its molecular composition and reactivity.
Explain metal binding and light attenuation without treating all organic matter as identical.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Operational fractions
Organic matter contains many molecules and particles with different sizes and functional groups. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is an operationally measured carbon amount after the specified separation; particulate organic carbon is associated with the retained fraction. Neither result gives a unique molecule, ligand concentration, or biodegradation rate. Record the filter and analytical method. Some colloidal material may appear in an operationally dissolved fraction.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Functional groups create reactivity
Carboxyl, phenolic, and other binding groups can lose protons and bind metals. Their charge and availability change with pH. Binding can keep a metal in a filtered fraction while lowering its free-ion concentration. Organic matter can also promote colloidal transport. Greater DOC therefore does not automatically mean lower total dissolved metal or no metal exposure; kinetics, uptake routes, and ligand chemistry matter.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Colour changes the light field
Chromophoric organic matter absorbs parts of the light spectrum. Darker water can reduce light penetration and alter where photochemical reactions occur. Not all DOC absorbs equally: colour per unit carbon varies with composition and processing. Absorbance is therefore a property measurement, not a direct universal conversion to DOC. Photochemical change can transform molecules without immediately removing all carbon from water.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Organic oxidation consumes oxygen
Use \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) as a stoichiometric representation of a simple organic substrate: \[\mathrm{CH_2O+O_2\rightarrow CO_2+H_2O}.\] One mole of its carbon consumes one mole of O₂ in complete aerobic oxidation. This is a teaching carbon-oxidation model, not the molecular formula of all natural organic matter. Real demand depends on oxidation state, biodegradability, timescale, and other oxygen-consuming processes such as nitrification.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Link to anoxia and sediment
When oxygen demand exceeds replenishment, oxygen can decline. Other electron acceptors may then support microbial oxidation. Reduction of iron-bearing solids can change sorption surfaces and release associated solutes. Reaeration, mixing, and photosynthesis can offset demand, so an organic-carbon increase is not itself a complete oxygen budget. Measure both the sources and sinks on an appropriate timescale.

title: Organic matter in water
text:
Worked example
Assume 3.00 mg C/L of an added CH₂O-like substrate is completely oxidised aerobically. With molar masses 12.0 g/mol for carbon and 32.0 g/mol for O₂, the demand is \(3.00(32.0/12.0)=\mathbf{8.00}\) mg O₂/L. That is an ultimate stoichiometric demand for this substrate. It is not a measured five-day biochemical oxygen demand, nor a prediction that all of a lake’s DOC is consumed immediately.

title: Chemical glossary
text:
Use these definitions with the model conditions in each unit. Similar words can describe different quantities; always check the phase and units.



Term
Meaning and explanation




Activity
Effective thermodynamic quantity relative to a standard state; concentration approximation.


Adsorption/sorption
Association with a surface or solid phase; phase balance. Sorption is the broader term used here.


Aerosol
Suspended solid particles or liquid droplets in air; deposition.


Alkalinity
An acid-neutralising balance in charge equivalents per volume; carbonate expression.


Bioavailability
Availability of chemical forms to a biological uptake or interaction process; speciation limits. It is not synonymous with a filtered total.


Buffer capacity
Resistance to a small pH change under specified conditions; distinction from alkalinity.


Cation exchange capacity
Exchange-site charge inventory per dry solid mass under stated conditions; CEC.


Charge equivalent
Amount weighted by ionic charge magnitude; charge balance.


Colloid
A small dispersed particle whose operational classification depends on method; particle transport.


Complex
A coordinated metal–ligand species; one-ligand model.


Concentration
Amount or mass per volume; inventory distinction.


Dissolved inorganic carbon
Carbon summed across the specified dissolved inorganic species; carbonate model.


Dissolved organic carbon
Organic carbon in a defined operational fraction; DOC.


Flux/load
Amount transferred per area per time or amount per time, respectively, with the convention stated; deposition budget.


Free ion
Uncomplexed aqueous ion in the stated model; metal total distinction.


Half-life
Time for half the tracked parent to transform under the specified kinetic model; first-order equation.


Henry coefficient
A convention-dependent gas–water equilibrium coefficient; units and pool.


Ionic strength
Half the sum of concentration times squared charge number; nonideality.


Kd
Solid-to-water distribution coefficient with the specified phase and concentration units; linear model.


Koc
Organic-carbon-normalised sorption coefficient for an appropriate model; conditional use.


Kow
Octanol–water distribution of a specified molecular form; property limitations.


Ligand
A binding partner coordinating a metal; free and total ligand.


Mineral saturation
Comparison of the free-ion activity product with equilibrium; calcite example.


Oxidation/reduction
Loss/gain of electrons; balanced half-reactions.


pH
Negative base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity; dilute approximation.


Photolysis
Light-driven molecular change following absorption; atmospheric chemistry.


Speciation
Distribution among chemical forms under stated conditions; ratios and fractions.


Steady state
Zero net accumulation despite continuing processes; balance.


Transformation
Change of chemical identity; parent and product distinction.

text:
Before interpreting a water analysis, can its reported concentrations satisfy charge balance, and which quantities belong in an equilibrium expression?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Learning goals

Convert ionic concentrations to charge equivalents.
Distinguish analytical totals, free concentrations, and activities.
Use an equilibrium model without confusing thermodynamic possibility with reaction speed.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Water is a reaction medium
Dissolved ions are hydrated; their interactions depend on charge, solution composition, and temperature. A formula in an analytical table may denote an element total, a specific ion, or a reporting convention. Read the method and units before calculating. A filtered metal result does not necessarily mean free metal ion; small complexes and some colloids can pass the chosen filter.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Charge balance is a constraint
Bulk water must be electrically neutral. Sum positive and negative ionic charge equivalents, not masses: \[\Sigma_+=\sum_{z_i>0}z_ic_i,\qquad\Sigma_-=\sum_{z_i<0}|z_i|c_i.\] Using mmol/L gives meq/L. A calcium concentration of 0.500 mmol/L contributes 1.00 meq/L because calcium is divalent. A mismatch suggests omitted ions, unsuitable speciation, reporting errors, or analytical uncertainty; the water itself has not become macroscopically charged.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Concentration and activity
Thermodynamic equilibrium constants use dimensionless activities. For an aqueous solute, write \(a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ\), with \(c^\circ=1\) mol/L and activity coefficient \(\gamma_i\). In dilute teaching examples we take \(\gamma_i\approx1\), making numerical concentrations convenient. Ionic strength \(I=\tfrac12\sum c_i z_i^2\) weights squared charge; divalent ions can influence nonideality strongly. The dilute approximation should not be carried unexamined into seawater.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
A simple acid distribution
For \(\mathrm{HA\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-}\) in the concentration approximation, \[\frac{[A^-]}{[HA]}=10^{\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}.\] If these are the only forms, the deprotonated fraction is \(r/(1+r)\). At a prescribed pH one unit above the pKa, the ratio is ten and the fraction is \(10/11\). The pH must come from a measurement or an additional balance; a distribution formula does not by itself solve for pH.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
A small redox bridge
Oxidation loses electrons and reduction gains them. For example, \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}+e^-\rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}\) changes oxidation state; binding a ligand without electron transfer does not. Both pH and redox can change metal speciation. An equilibrium prediction tells which state is favoured under specified conditions. Kinetics, access to reactants, and transport determine whether the state is reached in the sampling period.

title: Aquatic composition and equilibrium
text:
Worked example

Closure is a useful check, not proof that every concentration or species assignment is correct.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Light selects reactions
Photolysis uses absorbed light to break or change a molecule. Photon energy is \(E=hc/\lambda\): shorter wavelengths carry more energy, but a reaction still requires absorption by the molecule. Light availability changes with altitude, clouds, and time. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation; at ground level it is an oxidising pollutant. The same formula does not mean the same environmental setting.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Make stratospheric ozone
A simplified formation sequence is \[\mathrm{O_2}+h\nu\rightarrow2\mathrm{O},\] \[\mathrm{O+O_2+M\rightarrow O_3+M}.\] M is a collision partner that removes excess energy. Ozone also undergoes photolysis and reactions with atomic oxygen. Abundance reflects a production–loss balance plus transport; a fast turnover need not imply a small steady inventory.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
A chlorine catalytic cycle
Consider \[\mathrm{Cl+O_3\rightarrow ClO+O_2},\] \[\mathrm{ClO+O\rightarrow Cl+O_2}.\] Adding the steps cancels Cl and ClO and gives \(\mathrm{O_3+O\rightarrow2O_2}\). Chlorine is regenerated and can repeat the sequence until another reaction interrupts it. This is a representative gas-phase cycle, not the full mechanism of the polar ozone hole; polar chemistry also involves particle surfaces and different catalytic cycles.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Tropospheric cycling
In the basic photochemical cycle, NO₂ photolysis forms NO and O; the O atom forms O₃ with O₂ and a collision partner. But \(\mathrm{NO+O_3\rightarrow NO_2+O_2}\) consumes that ozone. These steps alone form a cycle without sustained net production. Peroxy radicals from oxidation of volatile organic compounds or CO can instead convert NO to NO₂ without consuming ozone, allowing net ozone production in appropriate conditions.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Rates and lifetime
For a loss reaction \(X+\mathrm{OH}\rightarrow\) products, \(R=k[X][\mathrm{OH}]\). If OH is treated as constant, the pseudo-first-order loss coefficient is \(k'=k[\mathrm{OH}]\) and the chemical lifetime is \(1/k'\). This approximation isolates one sink. Deposition, transport, changing sunlight, and competing reactions alter the observed atmospheric persistence. A catalyst is regenerated in a sequence, not present in unlimited amount or active forever.

title: Reactions in the atmosphere
text:
Worked example
Adding the two chlorine steps gives one ozone molecule and one atomic oxygen consumed for every two oxygen molecules produced. Cl and ClO cancel. Each completed cycle therefore removes one ozone molecule, but the number of cycles per chlorine atom depends on competing reactions and conditions. Stoichiometry by itself gives neither the cycle rate nor a global ozone loss.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Absorption requires a matching transition
A molecule interacts with infrared radiation when the radiation matches an allowed rotational/vibrational transition. A vibration is infrared active when it changes the molecular dipole moment. The symmetric molecule CO₂ has infrared-active bending and asymmetric stretching modes; being symmetric does not mean every vibration is inactive. Homonuclear diatomics such as N₂ and O₂ lack ordinary dipole-active vibrational absorption and are weak direct greenhouse absorbers under ordinary atmospheric conditions.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Earth emits at different wavelengths
The warm surface emits strongly in the thermal infrared, whereas incoming sunlight is concentrated at shorter wavelengths. Absorbing and emitting gases alter how energy moves through the atmosphere and escapes to space. Absorption is wavelength dependent. The role of a gas depends on its bands, abundance, altitude, and overlap with other absorbers; one peak height is not a complete climate metric.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Read a deliberately simple spectrum
Use the supplied teaching spectrum below as a diagram of the logic, not a measured gas spectrum. At 0.55 µm the model transmits 0.95 of the incident light; at 10 µm it transmits 0.20. For this absorbing-only example, the absorbed fractions are \(1-T=0.05\) and \(0.80\). Real atmospheres also scatter and emit. Comparing transmission without the incident energy spectrum cannot give total absorbed power.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
text:
Persistence has several timescales
A first-order sink gives \(C(t)=C_0e^{-kt}\), a lifetime \(\tau=1/k\), and a half-life \(t_{1/2}=\ln2/k\). These are useful for a single isolated loss process. Carbon dioxide exchanges with ocean and land reservoirs on several timescales, so one exponential atmospheric lifetime does not describe all of its response. A gas’s chemical lifetime is also different from the time over which the climate system responds.

title: Molecules, radiation, and climate
section: Particles absorb, scatter, and change clouds
text:
Particles absorb, scatter, and change clouds
Aerosols can scatter sunlight, absorb radiation, and affect cloud droplet formation. Their effect depends on composition, size, location, and the surrounding surface or cloud. A reflecting particle and an absorbing particle need not have the same influence. Oxidation can convert emitted gases to particles, linking air-pollution chemistry with radiation. Do not assign every aerosol a universal cooling sign or a gas-like persistence.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Define the quantity
Concentration divides amount by volume; it is not an inventory. Mass concentration might be mg/L, amount concentration mol/L, and an inventory mg or mol. Use a molar mass only when converting between mass and chemical amount. A sample with lower concentration can contain more solute if its volume is larger. Specify whether a result is reported as the element or as a compound: mg N/L and mg nitrate/L are different quantities.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Choose a boundary
A compartment is a specified volume such as a lake, a water sample, or the water plus sediment in a bottle. A flux crosses its boundary; a reaction can transform a species inside it. Write what lies inside the boundary before adding terms. Sorption removes a compound from water but does not remove it from a water-plus-sediment system. Transformation of a parent compound need not destroy its constituent elements.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Write a balance
For the amount \(M\) of a specified substance, \[\frac{dM}{dt}=\text{inputs}-\text{outputs}+\text{production}-\text{consumption}.\] Every term has amount/time units. For a well mixed constant-volume water body, an advective output is \(QC\), where \(Q\) is water flow and \(C\) is outlet concentration. The inflow and outflow volumes must also balance if volume stays fixed. A steady state sets accumulation to zero; it does not imply that input and output processes have stopped.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Separate mixing from reaction
When two waters mix without reaction or loss, add their inventories and divide by the combined volume. For flows at a junction, add loads and divide by total flow. This is a conservation prediction, not an equilibrium calculation. If the observed result differs, investigate sampling times, mixing, uncertainty, missing inputs, and chemical change. A concentration difference alone cannot isolate a reaction rate.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
A timescale is a model
The hydraulic replacement time is \(V/Q\) for constant volume and flow. It estimates a water-replacement scale, not the age of every molecule or the chemical lifetime of every solute. Under a well mixed model, flushing an initially present conservative solute with clean water gives an exponential decline. A reactive solute also depends on transformation, sorption, and exchange with other compartments.

title: Environmental amounts and balances
text:
Worked example
Mix 2.00 L at 3.00 mg/L with 1.00 L at 0.600 mg/L. The inventories are 6.00 and 0.600 mg. With additive volumes, no reaction, and no loss, the final inventory is 6.60 mg in 3.00 L, so the concentration is 2.20 mg/L. It is lower than 3.00 mg/L because of dilution; none of the tracked solute was destroyed.

title: Metal speciation and mobility exercises
text:
1. Reduce ligand
Keep MT = 2.00 µmol/L and β = 1.00 × 10⁶ L/mol but prescribe free L = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L. Calculate free and complexed M.






Hint





The product β[L] is dimensionless.









Worked solution





β[L] = 1.00. Free M = 1.00 µmol/L and ML = 1.00 µmol/L. Lower free ligand increases the free-metal fraction in this model.

title: Metal speciation and mobility exercises
text:
2. Check ligand excess
A proposed calculation uses MT = 2.00 µmol/L, total LT = 0.500 µmol/L, and assumes 1.818 µmol/L of 1:1 ML. Why is it impossible?






Hint





Each complex consumes one ligand; check the ligand balance.









Worked solution





The proposed complex amount exceeds all available ligand by more than threefold. ML cannot exceed 0.500 µmol/L. At least 1.50 µmol/L metal remains outside ML; solve coupled balances for an exact distribution.

title: Metal speciation and mobility exercises
text:
3. Hydroxide saturation
For fictitious M(OH)₂, take Ksp = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁶ and prescribed [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. Find saturated free M. A water has dissolved total 10.0 µmol/L and β[L] = 9.00. Is it saturated in the two-species model?






Hint





Calculate the free concentration before evaluating the product.









Worked solution





Free saturation concentration = 1.00 µmol/L. The water has free M = 10.0/(1 + 9.00) = 1.00 µmol/L, so it is saturated in the stated model. Using total metal directly would incorrectly imply a tenfold excess.

title: Metal speciation and mobility exercises
text:
4. Metal after acidification
A filtered metal concentration rises as pH falls, but oxidation-state measurements stay unchanged. Name plausible chemical mechanisms and what would distinguish them.






Hint





Consider surfaces, minerals, and protonation before proposing redox.









Worked solution





Acid can desorb metal, dissolve a metal-bearing phase, or protonate a ligand and redistribute its binding. Measure free and total metal, ligand/organic matter, major ions, solids, and pH. Unchanged oxidation state is compatible with all these processes.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
What does a dissolved metal total conceal, and how can complexation change solubility without changing the metal oxidation state?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Learning goals

Use a one-ligand equilibrium with an explicit free-ligand approximation.
Distinguish complexation, hydrolysis, precipitation, and redox.
Check a free-ion solubility condition before interpreting a metal total.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Specify the species
A dissolved metal may be a hydrated ion, a hydrolysis product, a ligand complex, or an operationally included small colloid. A species balance sums forms of the same element. Complexation changes coordination and can change charge; it does not require electron transfer. Fe(II) to Fe(III), in contrast, changes oxidation state. Use oxidation state and species identity separately.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
A transparent binding model
Take one complex, \(\mathrm{M+L\rightleftharpoons ML}\), and use the concentration-based teaching constant \(\beta=[ML]/([M][L])\). With ligand in sufficiently large excess, prescribe free \([L]\) and write \[M_T=[M]+[ML]=[M](1+\beta[L]).\] Then \([M]=M_T/(1+\beta[L])\). If binding appreciably depletes ligand, a second balance \(L_T=[L]+[ML]\) is needed. Substituting total ligand for free ligand without checking this approximation can overestimate binding.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
pH changes coordination
Water ligands can lose protons, schematically \(\mathrm{M^{2+}+H_2O\rightleftharpoons MOH^++H^+}\). Rising pH often favours hydrolysis; it can also deprotonate organic ligands, changing their binding capacity. The competing trends depend on the specific metal and ligand. An acidic shift can release metal from a surface or ligand without requiring oxidation of the metal.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Test mineral saturation with free ions
text:
Test mineral saturation with free ions
For the fictitious hydroxide \(\mathrm{M(OH)_2(s)\rightleftharpoons M^{2+}+2OH^-}\), saturation requires \([M^{2+}][OH^-]^2=K_{sp}\) in the dilute approximation. The free-ion saturation concentration is \(K_{sp}/[OH^-]^2\). Complexation can increase the dissolved total compatible with this free-ion limit. If the solution is supersaturated, a reaction may be favoured, but the rate and final state still require kinetics and balances.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
section: Mobility and exposure are separate questions
text:
Mobility and exposure are separate questions
Strong dissolved binding can reduce free-ion concentration while allowing metal to travel with mobile water or colloids. Conversely, binding to immobile solids can retain metal locally. Biological exposure depends on metal form, competition, uptake mechanism, and reaction rates. A simple free-ion calculation is a chemical comparison, not a universal toxicity or risk model.



Model free-metal fraction at prescribed free-ligand concentrations.

title: Metal speciation and mobility
text:
Worked example
For a fictitious M, use \(M_T=2.00\) µmol/L, \(\beta=1.00\times10^6\) L/mol, and prescribed free ligand \([L]=1.00\times10^{-5}\) mol/L. Then \(\beta[L]=10.0\), so free M is 0.1818 µmol/L and ML is 1.818 µmol/L. The two forms sum to 2.00 µmol/L. These supplied values are a generic teaching model, not measured constants for a named environmental metal.

Take foc = 0.0200 and Koc = 5000 L/kg organic C for a suitable neutral compound. Find Kd. What mistake results from entering 2.00 instead of 0.0200?

2. Ionisation
A fictitious organic acid has pKa 4.50. Find the neutral fraction at prescribed pH 4.50 and 6.50. Can a neutral-form Koc automatically describe total sorption in both waters?






Hint





Use 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)).









Worked solution





Neutral fractions are 0.500 and 0.009901. A neutral-form coefficient alone cannot describe the total charged-plus-neutral pool without an appropriate ionisation/sorption model.

3. Another half-life
For compound U in the worked example, find total and aqueous parent after 30.0 days. State what the model says about products.






Hint





Three half-lives leave one eighth of the starting parent.









Worked solution





Total parent = 0.125 mg; water contains 0.0625 mg, so Cw = 0.0625 mg/L. The model records parent transformation but does not specify product identity, product toxicity, or elemental mineralisation.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate exercises
section: 4. A decline is not a mechanism
text:
4. A decline is not a mechanism
Water parent concentration falls after sediment is added. What would distinguish sorption from transformation, and why does log Kow alone not answer the question?






Hint





Measure both phases and plausible products on a consistent time basis.









Worked solution





Track total parent across water, solids, and any gas phase, plus products and analytical recoveries. Sorption conserves parent across phases; transformation changes identity. Log Kow describes partition preference, not a measured degradation mechanism or rate.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate exercises
section: Activity C: a fate model in R
text:
Activity C: a fate model in R
Download compounds.csv, fate.R, and fate-report.Rmd into one folder. Read the input dictionary. Reuse readr, dplyr, ggplot2, and the R Markdown workflow. The new mathematical operation is exp(), the inverse of the natural logarithm.
The script creates a regular daily table for the two cases and evaluates:
remaining_fraction = exp(-k_per_day * time_days)
total_parent_mg = initial_parent_mg * remaining_fraction
water_mg_l = total_parent_mg / (water_volume_l + kd_l_kg * dry_solid_kg)
These lines are expressions used inside mutate() in the supplied script. The starting mass is already distributed between phases at time zero. The coefficient k applies equally to parent in water and solids; this assumption is what lets total parent follow one exponential.

Predict which compound has more parent in water initially. Calculate U’s day-20 state by hand before running the code.
Run source("fate.R"), inspect fate, and print fate_plot.
Check time zero, one half-life, and the sum of the two phase inventories.
Explain why a smaller water concentration does not automatically mean a shorter half-life, less total parent, or lower biological risk.
Complete the report, restart R, and Knit it from saved inputs. Use its final section to make the separate catchment and sediment arguments in the integrated case.







Expected model results





At day zero, U has 0.500 mg/L water parent and V has 0.9091 mg/L, because their Kd values differ. At day 20, U has 0.250 mg total parent, split equally between phases, giving 0.125 mg/L water concentration. At day 30, U has 0.125 mg total and 0.0625 mg/L water concentration; V has 0.500 mg total and 0.4545 mg/L water concentration.
The two parent phase inventories sum to the declining total. Total parent plus the transformed-parent accounting term equals the initial mass. The latter term records loss of parent identity, not a measured product mass or proof of mineralisation. These are model predictions under supplied constants, not a fit, a statistical comparison, or field evidence.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Which molecular properties help explain where a contaminant goes, and why is disappearance from water not the same as chemical destruction?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Learning goals

Relate ionisation and neutral partitioning to the stated environmental conditions.
Combine a two-phase balance with a supplied first-order parent-loss model.
Distinguish partitioning, persistence, exposure, and biological effect.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Structure affects phase preference
Nonpolar regions, hydrogen-bonding groups, size, and charge influence interactions with water and organic phases. The octanol–water coefficient \(K_{ow}\) compares concentrations of a specified form at equilibrium in two phases; log Kow is its base-ten logarithm. It is not a half-life or a toxicity measurement. Hydrophobic neutral compounds may associate strongly with organic matter, but uptake, metabolism, and environment still affect exposure.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Ionisation changes the problem
For a monoprotic organic acid HA, the neutral fraction is \[f_{HA}=\frac{1}{1+10^{\mathrm{pH}-pK_a}}.\] Rising pH shifts it toward A⁻. The neutral form and ion can have different sorption and uptake behaviour; a coefficient measured for neutral molecules may not describe the combined pool. Charged compounds can also bind strongly through ion exchange or specific interactions, so “ionised means no sorption” is not a valid general rule.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Use organic-carbon normalisation cautiously
For a suitable neutral organic solute in an organic-carbon-dominated sorption regime, use the approximation \(K_d=f_{oc}K_{oc}\), with organic-carbon fraction \(f_{oc}\) in kg organic C per kg dry solid and \(K_{oc}\) in L/kg organic C. This is a conditional approximation, not a rule for all ions, minerals, soot, or concentrations. Combining it with a water–solid mass balance predicts distribution only within those conditions.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
A first-order parent-loss model
With constant \(k\) and no new parent input, \[M(t)=M_0e^{-kt},\qquad k=\ln2/t_{1/2}.\] Mass here tracks the parent compound. Products may remain and need not be harmless or fully mineralised. A measured water decline could also result from sorption, volatilisation, or export; it does not establish this transformation model without supporting evidence. Rate coefficients depend on conditions and the process represented.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
State the coupled teaching model
In activity C, a closed water–solid system equilibrates rapidly at fixed Kd. Parent transformation acts with the same specified first-order coefficient in both phases, so the total parent mass follows one exponential. Then \(C_w(t)=M(t)/(V_w+K_dm_s)\). There is no volatilisation, inflow, or outflow. If only dissolved parent degraded or exchange were slow, this model would need a different kinetic balance.

title: Organic contaminants and environmental fate
text:
Worked example
For fictitious neutral compound U, take \(M_0=1.00\) mg, \(V_w=1.00\) L, \(m_s=0.0100\) kg, \(K_d=100\) L/kg, and half-life 10.0 days. Initially half the parent is in water and \(C_w=0.500\) mg/L. After 20.0 days the total parent is 0.250 mg; water and solid each contain 0.125 mg, so \(C_w=\mathbf{0.125}\) mg/L. The missing 0.750 mg parent has transformed under this stipulated model. It has not simply moved to the sorbed parent pool.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
1. Exchange amount
A 0.100 kg soil has CEC 20.0 cmolc/kg. If all sites were occupied by Mg²⁺, how many moles of Mg would occupy them?






Hint





Convert cmol of charge to mol of charge, then divide by two.









Worked solution





Total charge = 20.0 × 0.01 × 0.100 = 0.0200 mol charge. Mg²⁺ amount = 0.0100 mol. This is an idealised capacity state, not an aqueous concentration.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
2. Base saturation
A soil has CEC 12.0 cmolc/kg and base-cation occupation 9.00 cmolc/kg. Calculate base saturation. Does the result specify soil-water pH?






Hint





Divide occupied base charge by total exchange charge.









Worked solution





Base saturation = 75.0%. It does not uniquely set pH; mineralogy, exchange selectivity, solution composition, other acid–base reactions, and the measurement method matter.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
3. A carbonate inventory
A soil contains 0.0100 mol accessible CaCO₃. For a specified complete neutralisation endpoint, take CaCO₃ + 2 H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂* + H₂O. How much acid can this inventory consume?






Hint





Use the two-equivalent coefficient for the stated endpoint.









Worked solution





The stoichiometric inventory is 0.0200 mol H⁺ equivalents. Real protection also depends on dissolution rate, accessibility, gas exchange, and the actual final state.

title: Soil chemistry and retention exercises
text:
4. Compare two soils
Two soils have equal pH but one is rich in organic matter and exchange-active clay while the other is coarse quartz sand. What would you measure before predicting their responses to an acid input?






Hint





Measure inventories and pathways, not only pH.









Worked solution





Compare CEC under stated conditions, base saturation, carbonate and weatherable minerals, organic matter, water flow, and aluminium/iron chemistry. Equal pH is not evidence of equal buffering or solute retention.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Why can two soils at the same pH differ in their response to acid or a contaminant input?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Learning goals

Connect mineral and organic surfaces with exchange and buffering.
Calculate charge-based exchange inventories.
Explain why retention capacity does not determine transport by itself.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Several reacting phases
Soil contains minerals, organic matter, water, gas, and organisms. Water composition reflects contact with those phases and the time available for reaction. Soil pH measures a state under a specified method; it does not inventory exchange sites or neutralising minerals. Texture, mineralogy, organic matter, and flow paths therefore matter even when two pH measurements are equal.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Cation exchange conserves charge
A negatively charged exchange site can hold cations. A schematic exchange is \(\mathrm{2XNa+Ca^{2+}\rightleftharpoons X_2Ca+2Na^+}\), with X denoting one negative site charge. Exchange transfers ions between water and sites without destroying the element. A divalent ion occupies two monovalent charge equivalents. Selectivity depends on the exchanger, ion activities, and competing ions.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Interpret exchange capacity
Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is commonly reported as cmol of charge per kg dry soil, written cmolc/kg. One cmolc is 0.01 mol of charge equivalents. Permanent mineral charge and pH-dependent sites contribute differently, so method and pH matter. Base saturation expresses the fraction of exchange capacity occupied by specified base cations; it does not mean the solution has that same ion ratio.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
section: Acid inputs meet a finite inventory
text:
Acid inputs meet a finite inventory
Protons can displace cations, protonate organic and oxide sites, and dissolve minerals. A carbonate-bearing soil can consume acidity through mineral dissolution. An acid soil lacking carbonate may rely more on exchange, weathering, and aluminium chemistry. Some neutralisation reactions mobilise metals or change nutrient availability. A measured resistance to one short acid pulse does not guarantee indefinite protection under continued inputs.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Retention and preferential flow
A soil with many potential sites may still transmit solute through fast pathways with limited solid contact. Waterlogged microsites can change redox and the stability of iron phases. Colloids may transport sorbed substances, while erosion moves the solids themselves. To explain movement, combine chemical partitioning with water flow, residence time, and particle transport. Avoid using CEC as a universal sorption coefficient for anions or neutral organic compounds.

title: Soil chemistry and retention
text:
Worked example
A dry soil has CEC 10.0 cmolc/kg. In 0.200 kg, the exchange charge inventory is \(10.0\times0.01\times0.200=\mathbf{0.0200}\) mol of charge. If half is occupied by Ca²⁺, calcium carries 0.0100 mol charge and corresponds to 0.00500 mol Ca, not 0.0100 mol Ca. This capacity accounting is not a prediction that all that calcium immediately enters porewater.

1. Sum the reactions
Combine the two pyrite/iron stages and show the final oxygen and water coefficients.






Hint





Add equations and cancel Fe²⁺.

FeS₂ + 15/4 O₂ + 7/2 H₂O → Fe(OH)₃ + 2 SO₄²⁻ + 4 H⁺. Fe, S, O, H, and charge balance. The product charge is −4 + 4 = 0.

2. A shortfall
The worked pyrite inventory reacts fully, but only 0.0150 mol accessible CaCO₃ is available. Calculate the residual acid equivalents for the stated endpoint.






Hint





Subtract two equivalents per mole of accessible calcite from the generated amount.









Worked solution





Acid generated = 0.0400 mol eq; neutralised = 0.0300 mol eq; residual = 0.0100 mol eq. Final pH still requires a water volume and the remaining acid–base equilibria.

Discharge A is 10.0 L/s with dissolved Fe 2.00 mg/L. Discharge B is 40.0 L/s with Fe 1.00 mg/L. Which exports more iron?

Multiply each concentration by its own flow.

4. Long-term claim
A treated waste initially gives neutral-pH water. What evidence is needed before concluding that future metal and acid release will stay low?






Hint





Consider remaining reactive inventories, access, rate, and stability.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Why can a waste material continue producing acidity after the initial dissolved acid has been washed away?
Read these notes with the lecture, then complete the exercises. Numerical examples are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly described otherwise.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Learning goals

Balance sulfide oxidation and subsequent iron hydrolysis.
Distinguish present pH from potential acid-generating inventory.
Close a neutralisation budget and track the residual solids.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Expose a reactive mineral
Breaking and moving sulfide-bearing material changes access to oxygen and water. Pyrite oxidation can be represented by \[\mathrm{FeS_2+\tfrac72O_2+H_2O\rightarrow Fe^{2+}+2SO_4^{2-}+2H^+}.\] This first stage yields iron(II), sulfate, and acidity. Microbial and mineral-surface processes can affect rates. The presence of pyrite does not by itself give a discharge concentration without reaction extent, flow, and neutralisation terms.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
section: Iron oxidation can release more acid
text:
Iron oxidation can release more acid
Iron(II) can oxidise and precipitate as an idealised hydroxide: \[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}+\tfrac14O_2+\tfrac52H_2O\rightarrow Fe(OH)_3(s)+2H^+}.\] Adding this step to the initial pyrite oxidation gives four H⁺ equivalents per mole of pyrite for this endpoint. Real iron solids differ in hydration and crystallinity; the hydroxide notation is a teaching representation. Removing orange iron precipitate is not necessarily the end of acid generation.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Neutralisation is another reaction
For the specified CO₂* endpoint, \[\mathrm{CaCO_3+2H^+\rightarrow Ca^{2+}+CO_2^*+H_2O}.\] An inventory of calcite can consume acidity, but access, surface coatings, and dissolution rate can limit the realised effect. At other solution conditions, bicarbonate can remain and alter the net stoichiometric accounting. Always state the endpoint rather than treating one acid-neutralisation coefficient as independent of the chemical state.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Present acidity and future generation
A leachate pH is a snapshot. Remaining sulfide can continue oxidising; remaining minerals can continue neutralising. A high-flow period can dilute concentrations while exporting a large load. Assess acid generation, neutralisation inventories, and water flow together. Laboratory extraction conditions and duration should be reported because a short leach test may not represent long-term exposure.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Immobilisation can be reversible
Iron precipitates can retain metals or phosphate, but changed pH or redox can destabilise the retention. A waste treatment that transfers contaminants into solids needs a statement about the conditions keeping those solids stable. The same logic applies beyond mine waste: organic wastes can impose oxygen demand, and mixed wastes can change pH, ligand concentrations, and redox. Leachate chemistry is controlled by reactions as well as original composition.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
Worked example
Assume 0.0100 mol FeS₂ oxidises completely to sulfate and Fe(OH)₃ as represented above. It generates 0.0400 mol acid equivalents and 0.0200 mol sulfate. Neutralising that acidity to the stated CO₂* endpoint needs 0.0200 mol CaCO₃, or 2.00 g with supplied molar mass 100 g/mol. This is a stoichiometric comparison, not a field treatment dose: rates, mixing, other reactions, and residuals are omitted.

title: Waste materials and leachate chemistry
text:
